Here, you will see a letter of the assistant Foreign Minister of the Republic of Croatia addressed to General Wahlgreen, and I would like to ask you the following. Through your own channels of communication, were you informed about the arrival of this delegation and had you been given certain assignments in relation to that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DV [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't know about this document. We received orders to prepare the meeting on the 29th of April for a future visit. That's what we were ordered to do and that's what we did.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Very well. Now, when you see this letter, do you relate it in any way to that order, this meeting? Is it obviously the same topic, the same story, so to speak?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, obviously, it speaks of a multi-party parliamentary visit, and it's a visit of goodwill to the region, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: And you then took part in the preparations for and realisation of that visit; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct, my responsibility was to make sure that the meeting room, the necessary interpreters, the security measures, were all operational and functional, yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Thank you. But let's leave details aside. The core of the matter is that you participated. That's what matters. So did this visit actually take place?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Tell me, in relation to the further realisation of that visit, did you have any role to play, or did you have any assignments in terms of opening contacts with the other side too, the Muslim side, that this delegation also wished to speak to?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DV [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I remember rightly, no. I think they did that themselves.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Do you remember that there were certain problems when the delegation asked for certain contacts with the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina and East Mostar? Were you supposed to provide a security escort for them? Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DV [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't take part in that part. I know that there it was a problem but I wasn't part of that. I think the commission did actually go across to the other side.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: All right. So you cannot discuss details, but you remember that they did cross over to the other side as well, and that there were some problems in that regard. We can agree on that, can we not, without going into any further detail?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. To the best of my memory, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You talked to the people who worked on preparing this visit, like you, I'm primarily referring to the people from the HVO and then the delegation themselves when they arrived. During these contacts, did you learn of some information to the effect that this goodwill mission took place, the visit of this delegation took place, at a previous initiative of General Praljak's in Zagreb? Did you hear anything about that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DV [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Also in terms of the realisation of this, did you learn that the Republic of Croatia also officially notified the Bosnian authorities about this through their embassy?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DV [Resumed]
utterances.text: I suppose. That it is a standard procedure.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: I would like to ask that you look at the next document in my binder. That is 3D 01092.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DV [Resumed]
utterances.text: I understand, 091?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: 01092. You will see the exact number on the screen. We see a diplomatic note here sent by the Ministry of Foreign Affairs of the Republic of Croatia to the embassy of Bosnia-Herzegovina and the Republic of Croatia, the same persons are referred to, information is provided on that same visit. Can you link that up with this visit as well?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DV [Resumed]
utterances.text: I understand that, yes, that this refers to the same people, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Let us just go through a minor point here. In the paragraph we already referred to, paragraph 24 in your statement from 2007, and yesterday, the day before yesterday, you said that you heard about this, or rather that you knew about it from the newspapers. It was your understanding that General Praljak was the chief of the Main Staff of the Croatian army. You said yesterday that you actually learned about this from the newspapers. Can you assert that that was the post he held or was that just your impression?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DV [Resumed]
utterances.text: The impression that I had was not based on direct contact with him, because I didn't have any at that time. It's just what I read in the local press about him.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Very well. I'm going to show you a document now, P1889 [as interpreted]. It's also close to this one. It's the fourth document in my binder. You have two documents here.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DV [Resumed]
utterances.text: I found it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: So from these documents, you can see that in the same month, in April 1993, the position held by General Praljak in the Ministry of Defence in Croatia is quite different. He is assistant Defence Minister for political activity.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PRANDLER
utterances.text: Mr. Kovacic, I'm sorry to interrupt you, only one small issue of the transcript. In your -- when you referred to the your document, I believe it should have been P1859, but in the transcript, it is P1889. So the P1889 should be corrected as P1859. That one is --

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You're right, Your Honour. The witness is looking at the right document so it's actually two documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Witness, now that you saw that the position of General Praljak is described in a completely different way, can you agree that your idea at the time that he was chief of General Staff of the Croatian army at the time was wrong?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DV [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as we knew, we based our idea on the local press, and the local press talked of a high-ranking officer of the chief of Main Staff, and we saw that he was an important person. But it's irrelevant to me whether or not my idea was correct or not. At the time, I believed, and the press coincided in that he was a member -- chief of Main Staff. So my attitude toward General Praljak doesn't actually change.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Witness, my question is a simple one. You had the idea that you had, and you've just repeated it for the second time. I'm showing you a document, proof that your idea was obviously wrong. My question is do you agree now that you see this well-founded document that asserts something completely different? Was your initial assessment wrong, yes or no? We know, we understand, why it was that your initial assessment was wrong but it's just yes or no.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You told us and it is beyond doubt from your statements that the area of responsibility of responsibility of the Spanish Battalion in Bosnia-Herzegovina at the time included inter alia the area of Jablanica; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DV [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In your statement, in the first one, in 1997, for example, on page 8, English number 4, you don't have to look at it now, I'm going to remind you, you said that actually you did not know what the quality of the information was that you, in the SpaBat, gathered in the field, but certainly the quality of information improved over time because you came in April when the conflict just started. So this is a general assessment that you made. Do you stand by it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DV [Resumed]
utterances.text: In any process where people are involved, depending on the people who get to know the situation better, the quality of the information received and disseminated improves. So therefore I can say the same for this situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you. In accordance with what you confirmed just now, you, I mean SpaBat, I'm referring to SpaBat, not to you personally, did you have any information about Croat victims in Doljani, in the area of Jablanica, on the 28th of July 1993, when 63 persons were killed, massacred? Did you hear of this incident? Because I cannot find it anywhere in your reports.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not all details are necessarily going to be included in all reports. This was a well-known -- if this was a well-known incident to my SpaBat, then it -- everyone would have known about it. I don't know if the date was right or the number of people were right, but I know that officials in our company were informed. I received a document concerning the Croatian victims, and this was in English, and it went to the UNHCR, if I remember correctly, but the details of these incidents are no longer in my memory right now.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Very well. Let's not go into any greater detail because you're not aware of any detail. Also, practically there is no information in the SpaBat reports about an incident that took place on the 8th of September 1993, that is to say at the time when you were supposed to have better information. In the village of Grabovica, can you tell us something about that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DV [Resumed]
utterances.text: I go back to what I said before. I don't have in my head everything -- all the details of what happened in different towns or villages. I'm sure the information would have been there at the time. But all the information that SpaBat had at that time was verified and then sent to the relevant authorities and to the NGOs concerned. We had no reservations in -- we did not hold back any relevant information. That I can stipulate. Personally, I was involved in handing in a document that you gave us concerning certain massacres that took place. I can say that much.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Nevertheless, I would like to ask you to look at document 3D 00936. The fifth or sixth document in this binder. The fifth or the sixth one. Oh, you found it. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, the fifth, I have it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: We don't have time to show you more documents but please look at this information written by a Bosnian army commander in Konjic in September 1993, and he writes about what he learned at that point in time about the incident. Does this jog your memory? Because you did say that you had this information to a degree.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DV [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is the first time that I've read this document. I think that it refers to elements related to that incident.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you. Let's not go into this any further. It won't be necessary. Just another small question. In your report, P04401, that you have in the Prosecution binder, but you don't have to look at it now, you will remember, some information is referred to, that is to say the report of the 20th of August 1993, stating that a certain Juka had been relieved of his command and expelled from the HVO. Do you know who this Juka was?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I remember that in the second section, they showed me some photos that they had. They also called him "El Rubio," in Spanish, the blond one. And I remember that someone told us that he had been expelled from the HVO. Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Did you perhaps receive any more information? I'm going to put the Defence proposition to you and then you tell me. Did you ever find out that General Praljak, in agreement with Mr. Stojic, that is to say the Defence department, and with the approval of Boban, ordered that Juka be relieved of his command and expelled from the HVO precisely due to lack of discipline? Have you heard about that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DV [Resumed]
utterances.text: I hadn't heard of that, but I'm pleased to hear that, if that was the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you. For the record, I would just like to deal with the following. Similar information is contained in P2902. Juka is mentioned there as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, by your leave, I would like to cede the floor to Mr. Praljak now so that he puts a few questions in this regard. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Mr. Praljak?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: Good afternoon, Your Honours. Good afternoon, sir. Of course, I shall abide by the instructions given by the Trial Chamber and stick to technical military questions only and things that have to do with me personally. Sir, let us go back to the 11th of May 1993. You were stopped at a curve right by the entrance into the town of Mostar when you were going to help a soldier of yours; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DV [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: Before I continue, due to the volume of material that I have to deal with, I'm going to put very technical military specific questions, so please, without providing any big explanations, give me answers that are as short as possible to those questions. Is it correct that at that point in time, I came by in my car on my own, alone?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. You appeared quickly.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: When you say "quickly," it seems that you called me, but we were not communicating. As far as I can remember, I just happened to come by. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DV [Resumed]
utterances.text: My understanding was that I was asking for some authority or commander to come when you appeared. To my understanding, it was a gift from the heavens. You were the solution I was hoping for. Whether or not it was planned or chance, I actually can't say. But you appeared, that is true, and in my declaration, I said that I was stopped and you appeared.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: Thank you very much. So we are not going to go into that now, who was called and how it came to my arrival. Did you pass by? Did I -- did I have to behave as if I were in a parlour or did I have to yell and scream in order to get my point across?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DV [Resumed]
utterances.text: I lost part of the interpretation but I'm reading it. You did raise your voice at some point, but the people who were there present obeyed you as if by instincts. They obeyed you naturally and I was very surprised. It's clear that they had no doubt, you said let them go through, and we went through. That was very clear.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: Just another question in relation to this topic. Do you know what I was doing in that area in the spring and summer of 1992? Did you know any of that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DV [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know it.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Now, well, sir, you had a look at these documents that are Prosecution documents, and you testified to their authenticity. Now, through some of these documents -- well, I'd like to go through some of these documents quickly. You don't have to look at them. I'm just going to ask you about some things that are contained in these documents, whether you personally know about that. Not what these documents actually state. Of course, the honourable Judges have that. They will read that. When you saw me there on the 11th, was I wearing a camouflage uniform and on the basis of what did you conclude that I was a member of the HV, the Croatian army, at the time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DV [Resumed]
utterances.text: The first observation that I made of you was that you were wearing the uniform. It wasn't a field uniform, but it was just a general uniform of the Croatian army. That's why I thought that you were a high-ranking officer of the Croatian army, and we said among ourselves that -- that you are one of Tudjman's close aides. I also stated in my statement that I remember more your face than your uniform. I remember your facial characteristics. I also remember, on the 16th, when I made my report concerning the events surrounding the lieutenant, I made those statements.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: Sir, in your statement you do not say that I told you that I was one of Tudjman's men. Did I tell you there that place, that I was Tudjman's man or where?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DV [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, no, no. I never said that. I said that in the local press, and through the interpreters, the impression that I got was that you were one of Tudjman's most important men, or one of the most important Croatian military men. That was the idea. Until the 11th of May, I had never met you, never spoken with you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: Thank you. Now take a look at your first statement, or rather, you don't have to look at it, I'll read it out. This is what you said. "I'm convinced that the presence of General Pasalic in Mostar was not just by chance. General Pasalic was perhaps there because he was conscious of the fact that there would be an HVO attack." That's on page 8 of the Croatian text. And then it goes on to say that the Muslims had a good intelligence service which was infiltrated into the -- had infiltrated the structures of the HVO. So Pasalic was there because he was fully conscious of the fact that there would be an attack on the HVO. Now, in your second statement, 39, you say, "Initially they did not want to allow them to enter Mostar. They wanted them to take the direction to Dracevo." That's what you say in paragraph 39. It was only after these talks with Bozic that they could finally enter Mostar. And Their Honours have heard about this. My position was that Pasalic should have been authorised in. The Croat part, counterpart, should not be prevented from moving freely. And then an important sentence follows: "In my opinion, Pasalic's presence in Mostar on time could have prevented the conflict." So we're dealing with the 9th of May 1993, and in a paragraph that I've read out, it says that Pasalic was there because he was aware of the fact that there would be a HVO attack, and the second time, it is claimed that the presence of Pasalic in Mostar could prevent the conflict. Now, is that a contradiction? I think it's quite obvious we needn't analyse it further, but is it obviously a contradiction, written in this way? No explanations are necessary, just as it stands, is it a contradiction?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DV [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that -- I can't hear. I don't think this is a contradiction, Your Honour, because each sentence has its own stand-alone meaning. I'm not getting into the conflict on the 9th but if I were leader of one band --

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: Witness, please, I do apologise, but on the 9th of May -- well, the conflicts -- please. If you say it's not a contradiction, that is enough for me. I just don't have the possibility, because of the time constraints, to go into that. If you say it wasn't a contradiction, it wasn't a contradiction, right. My next question is this: If, as is claimed in the documents, the HVO attacked on the 9th of May, the BH army, how, then, would the timely presence of Pasalic have prevented -- how could the presence of Pasalic, a soldier of the 4th Corps, could have prevented this attack, the HVO, if the HVO had decided to attack? Then Pasalic's presence couldn't have prevented this, could it? So would it be logical, judging by this sentence, that the Pasalic's presence could have prevented the BH army from attacking the HVO on the 9th of May? Might it have been that way around?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DV [Resumed]
utterances.text: In my opinion, no. In my opinion, in my opinion if Pasalic had been there, maybe the HVO would not have attacked, and he came quickly because there was an attack.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: Sir -- sir, please, the HVO attack, launched this large scale action when it saw that Pasalic wasn't there, otherwise it wouldn't have attacked because Pasalic was there, that's what you're saying? All right, fine. Now, take a look at document 22 -- just a moment, please, 2241, P02241, actually.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Sorry, please excuse me Mr. Praljak. Please excuse me. In the transcript, I noted what I conceive as a contrast or a contradiction between page 13, paragraph 24, when it is written that Mr. Pasalic was in Mostar because of an HVO attack; whereas, a little bit farther down, page 14, I think, it is line 3 or something like that, it is written an attack on the HVO. And the first time one thinks if one reads it that the HVO would attack, and the second time that the HVO would be the object of an attack. I think it would be useful if this could be clarified. THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation] My question, as I put it, was simple. If somebody claims that the presence of Pasalic in Mostar would prevent an attack, then my question, based on that fact is this: The commander of the 4th Corps can prevent an attack of his own army, the 4th Corps commander of the BH army can't prevent an attack of the HVO, particularly such a large-scale attack on a town like that. So I was going to ask the witness whether he thinks that is logical. And the fact that what is claimed is that the fact that Pasalic isn't there created and led to an attack. So quite obviously it was a BH army attack because when the opposite army opposing army decides to attack, it must prepare for an attack and as Judge Antonetti asked, it means a lots of troop movement, logistics movement. It's not just three houses in a village. So that was my question. But as the witness does not feel that there is any contradiction that Pasalic is in Mostar or not in Mostar, then unfortunately not because I wouldn't like to clarify the point but because of my time constraints, and I have to get through a lot of things, then I'd like us to move on and look at 2241, P02241, the next document, please. It's page 3 of the Croatian text, 1, 2, and it's the Mostar area.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I have it. THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: You have found it, 2241?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: Just witness sentence I want to read out here and it this: Under Mostar, the heading of Mostar, it says, "Shelling" and then it goes on to say, "At 0500 hours from the positions of [indiscernible] an attack on the Muslim sector, the HVO forces broke through and reached the Muslim part of the Bulevar." So the HVO forces broke through and reached the Muslim part of the Bulevar. Now, as we can't get a military expert to testify here or haven't as yet, I'm asking you, as a soldier, if the separation line was at the Bulevar before that, then how -- now, on the 9th of May 1993, against what forces did the HVO have to break through to reach the Bulevar? Unless somebody had passed the line towards the HVO and then the HVO forces in their turn managed to reach the Bulevar again and break through the opposing army's forces. Is what I'm saying logical? And is that the sentence? It says "They broke through and reached the Bulevar. " THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation] Now, Your Honours, I'd like to remind you of another document. Thank you, where it was stated that the BH army forces were withdrawing to the Bulevar, but I haven't got time to go into that.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. Now take up my set of documents, my binder. I think your answer was yes; is that correct? Did you say "yes," witness?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Which of the questions -- Witness, please, in the indictments, the date of the 9th of May is a critical one. This is the reason why for nearly over 18 months this is a recurrent date. You yourself, where were you on the 9th of May?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] On the 9th of May, I was in the Medjugorje headquarters. I was woken up at 6.30 in the morning, and we were told that there were attacks in Mostar. We got the chain of commander up and running, we received information from the units that we had in the area, they had to leave the area and that's where activities began, from about 8.00 in the morning when we had a first meeting with the colonel, and we met together with the NGOs who had also left the area, and I think by 8.00 that night we were in Mostar with the ambassador so yes, we were aware of the situation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] At the level of SpaBat, the analysis that you had to carry out of the events as they were occurring, what did it say? Did you think it was a HVO attack or was it an ABiH attack? What was your estimation? Based on the information you had.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, in the INTREP that Mr. Praljak mentioned it says, and this was signed at 8.00 that evening, it says shelling at 5.00 in the morning. There were attacks, mortar attacks, on the Muslim areas by HVO and from there, the situation developed. So from the beginning, we had some doubt because it seemed a little bit contradictory. We heard from the HVO that it was the ABiH was attacking and so we -- yes?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] One moment. This is the first time I've been hearing this. You are saying that there were ABiH officials that called you? HVO officials, who called you to say that it was the ABiH that was attacking. This is the first time I'm hearing this. Who called from the HVO to say that it was an ABiH attack?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The information came from people in the field who had contacts with HVO elements, who were the ones saying that there was shelling. I can't recall -- I personally did not receive that information because it was not part of our mandate. However, during the first two hours we did not know who had started the shelling because it was in the midst of battle. We didn't know. As time went on, the incognito, in fact, was dissipated. THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: Sir, it says here a mortar attack was carried out. Now, a mortar, is it an anti-infantry weapon, first and foremost, that is to say a weapon most frequently used to prevent the penetration of certain forces so when forces are out in the open and when they are attacking, mortars are used, are they not, against infantry men, against an infantry attack? Would this be correct militarily speaking?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Against defenceless infantry.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: Now, that's right, yes, yes. Now, take up my binder that you've been given, and let's open it to the last document, 3D 00628.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DV [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've got it.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: The 10th of May 1993 is the date of the document. And it says, the conflicts in Mostar -- well let me ask you this: Do you know about Mr. Andric, that he was a member of the Main Staff of the HV at the time? Have you heard of the name, Miro Andric? He negotiated with you.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I did meet Colonel Andric. He came with me to Jablanica to solve some of the HVO -- some of the HVO problems.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. Now, let's focus on this. He says, "These conflicts began with an attack on the 9th of May at 0500 hours, with an attack of the BH army against the Tihomir Misic barracks. Also the Muslim forces attempted to break through and reach the building of the Office of the President of the HZ HB and that was successfully repulsed." And so on and so forth. Well, it goes on to say that there are a large number of false information, a large number of false information being disseminated through Radio Sarajevo. Did you hear about any of this from your men, that the BH army reached the Rondo and deep into the HVO lines and a barracks where Mate Boban was at the time or rather, the office building of the president of the HZ HB, Mate Boban? Do you know about any of this? If not, I'd just like to go through the document, sir?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, there is an interruption here, the number of the document is 4D, 4D 00628.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. I remember perfectly that I received information at the command post whereby we knew that the building of the Presidency where Mate Boban had been lodged from the night before had been attacked. Yes, I remember that comment. THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. Now take a look at the next document, the third from the end, 3D 00898. It is a document dated the 7th of May, that is to say two days before the clashes. Did you know -- 3D --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Just a moment. I do not have that document.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: 3D 00898. It is the third from the bottom in my set of documents.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Fine, fine.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: Do you know anything at all about the things mentioned in this document, that is to say that in the afternoon, as it states in the last sentence, the BH army police took away 13 HVO members from the point mentioned, and this is a BH army document, sir. Please note that, a BH army document. Do you know anything about that? About the incidents -- incidents like this that took place earlier on, where, from joint check-points, people were taken away? Now what happened to them, we can't go into that now, but do you know about any of this?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DV [Resumed]
utterances.text: I recall that the HVO headquarters informed us at times that these things had taken place. We did not get details, but we knew there had been problems at check-points with BH elements.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, before I continue, is it true that on the 25th of August 1993, I, together with you, on your APC, took through a humanitarian convoy to the BH army check-point at the entrance to Mostar?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, completely correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: Sir, you're a military man. Now I'd like to go through a series of documents with you signed by Brigadier Miljenko Lasic, the commander of the operative zone in which Mostar is located. Well, do you know Mr. Miljenko Lasic. Let me ask you that first. You've written about him so I assume you've heard the name.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, of course I do know Brigadier Lasic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: Thank you. Now after we go through the documents I'll ask you a question at the end so let's look at 3D 01006 first, please. It's the ninth document from the beginning, dated the 9th of May 1993, "Based on the development of the situation in the town of Mostar," so the person who should lead the HVO attacks says, "In view of the developments, orders that 120 well-armed and trained men be urgently sent to Mostar and that they should report to" so and so, et cetera, and this was sent to the first Knez Domagoj Brigade and the Stjepan Radic fourth HVO Brigade. Is that what it says in this document from Milenko Lasic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it's what I can read in the English version of the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: Yes. That will suffice. Now look at the next document 3D 01009 is the document number. And in fact it's the next document that you come upon. Once again the date is the 9th of May and once again it was sent to the 4th HVO Brigade, and he is asking that PZO anti-aircraft Defence weapon be sent 14.5 millimetre along with 3.000 rounds of ammunition. Is that what it says there, sir?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: Now, let's look at the next document, 3D 01023. Once again dated the 9th of May 1993 signed by Miljenko Lasic, brigadier, issues an order to immediately send to Mostar six ambulance teams with vehicles. Once again, it says who to report to. Is that what it says, six ambulance teams with vehicles?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DV [Resumed]
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: Next document, please, sir.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: 3D 01008 is the document number, dated the 9th of May once again, 1993. Once again, it is Brigadier Lasic issuing an order to the 4th Brigade to urgently send a T-34 tank crew, that's an old Russian tank, this T-34, and he says that they should report to the commander of the tank battalion, is that what it says?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It's correct. All these documents are from the 9th of May.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: Thank you. And now on to the next document, 3D 01007.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DV [Resumed]
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: Once again the date is the 9th of May 1993. The same story, urgently send to Mostar a mortar platoon --

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: I must object. I don't understand the point of these questions. To read the documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] One moment. Well, the relevance is quite clear. It's absolutely relevant. Why do you raise an objection?

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: But I don't hear any questions to the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, but the witness cannot answer as to the documents, but I'm sure that a question will be put to him that sums up all the don't. At least that's what I suppose. Mr. Praljak? THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation] Yes, quite right, Your Honour. My question will be a clear question at the end. The gentleman is a soldier -- well, I can ask my question straight away, so he can think about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: If somebody were to see these documents of the 9th of May and the other documents that I'm going to read out, would the commander who was supposed to lead an operation against the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and an attack against a town in the morning, in the morning hours, would he write a document like this in which he is asking for all the possible weapons, mortar, tanks, ambulances, because his men are dying and so on. So my question is a military one, although we've never brought in a military expert here to testify, but I want to show that even a layman would find it quite clear, a military layman, that either an idiot would launch an attack like that. And if it wasn't a mad man then there was no HVO attack because these documents quite obviously show the kind of situation that the commander found himself on the 9th of May and that will be my question at the end after we've looked through all the documents. Now let's go on to the next document, 3D 00107 dated the 9th of May again. Where once again Mico Lasic is issuing an order to send him a 120 millimetre mortar platoon and some light rocket launchers, 107-millimetre ones. So is this a document that you can see in front of you now, sir?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, I can see the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, take a look at 3D 01001, the next document, please. The 9th of May is the date, the report was at 2100 hours. It starts with a chronology of events at 1420 hours because the rest of it seems to be lost and here Miljenko Lasic is reporting on what actually happened. At 1420 hours such and such a person was killed, he was forced to attack the cinema, the Partizan cinema, and Vicjina [phoen] Street. Now do you know that the Partizan cinema and Vicjina Street were at the very separation line between the HVO and BH army?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I remember that was said.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: Now, let's look at the end of this document. It says the general situation in Mostar is very difficult and the fighting is still going on, the HVO will try to fortify positions on the Bulevar. So it says. The general situation very difficult and the HVO will try to fortify its -- the positions along the Bulevar. So if somebody is trying to fortify and strengthen positions at the Bulevar at 1400 hours, which was the separation line, then would you, sir, and your professional soldier, exclude the fact that somebody had already broken through towards the eastern part of town? Or, rather, what I want to say is this: Towards the western part of town, whereas somebody is trying to fortify positions that he had earlier and did not expect an attack? Is that quite clear from what it says here? Can we understand that in any other way than I have just put to you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Having a look at these documents, which I see for the first time, I see the major problem faced by Major Lasic, whether you were the ones that led the offensive or whether it was the Armija, and the solutions adopted to wit to request men, well trained and armed, and artillery, and the information that arrived at SpaBat, if you're interested, Your Honour, in how I interpreted key events on the 9th of May, we understood that you, with your weaponry, were better organised. But when it comes to the infantry, perhaps the Armija infantry attained some immediate successes locally. If you look at the death toll, we are talking about six killed and 17 wounded people. So there were problems, major problems in Mostar. We are talking about the beginning of hostilities. In the different documents signed by brigadier Lasic, the other documents in which he asked for weaponry, he also issued orders to close a number of roads. Quite so. I agree with you, General Praljak, that it's not quite normal for somebody who is supposedly prepared an offensive on the very same day of the offensive to request support troops. The logic that you are following is crystal clear. But this does not exclude that I support the information that SpaBat provided via the chain of command on the basis of the information that we had at the time which is of course not these documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Witness -- if you just allow, witness, you have emitted now a hypothesis, what could be the explanation for this? Would another hypothesis be that an attacker is surprised, taken by surprise because he meets with much more resistance than he had expected, for instance, for bad intelligence.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, we believed that is what happened. We believed that the side that did not lead the attack did acquire a tactical low-level tactical advantage at the infantry level. It is not usual for an attack of the BH infantry would take place against the building in which the Presidency of Mate Boban was housed. That's not normal. There was a tremendous lack of foreplanning, forward planning, but these are conjectures that I'm not about to make 14 years later. That's not my responsibility.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, you are a senior officer and usually you are able to answer military-type questions. Following the documents that have been submitted to you, we are in the very heart of the military issue. There are two theses. One which is the case by the Prosecution that says that on the 9th of May at 5.00, the HVO attacked the headquarters of the 4th Corps and took the Vranica building. That's the Prosecution case. On the other hand, you have the case put forward by General Praljak, based on document 4D 628, a document from Colonel Andric, sent to Tihomir Blaskic, who commands the Central Bosnia operational zone, also telling what happened. So the scenario presumably is the following. At 5.00, the ABiH attacked the Tihomir Misic barracks, but they are successfully repulsed. Then the HVO, as a counteroffensive, is going to take the building in which the headquarters of the 4th Corps is located. So as part of this scenario, we have a series of documents showing that not on the 7th, not on the 8th, but on the 9th of May, a tank is being called urgently, as well as ambulances, material, equipment, and these documents might suggest that then, led by Mr. Lasic, there is a military system that is put in place to face the ABiH attack. You, you were not in Mostar proper, but outside Mostar. Which of these two scenarios do you think is more credible, the more sort of true-to-military-doctrine?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, if you refer to the Andric document there are two things that should not escape your attention. It's an answer to a request and it's signed on the 10th of May, that's to say the following day. Mention is made of the 5.00 in the morning attack and that a number of front lines and attacks against the presidential building have taken place but were repelled, and that the Armija building was taken over by the HVO including the 4th Corps building which was in the Croat zone, and that there is false information being aired by Sarajevo Radio. If this is all the basis to state that they did not take the initiative, I do not believe that it's successively accurate. The UNPROFOR analysed in situ, and we even had some people infiltrated to see what was actually happening with the shots, and on the very same day, on the 9th, not the 10th, we said that we understood that the initiative had been taken by the HVO. Having said this, I also agree with General Praljak's position to say, well, what sort of foreplanning was there within the HVO troops if they had to request more things on that very same day. The documents of Lasic have no time given, so we don't know; whereas, the UNPROFOR documents always, always, state the time. Both the time and the date and these for military purposes. But of course it's not up to me to judge this. In my opinion, and to answer your question, Your Honour, the criterion of the Defence which coincides with the information that UNPROFOR provided in the area on the same day of the attack is more consistent than the position adopted by General Praljak and his Defence counsel.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I'm sorry, witness, is this indeed what you want to say, that the point of the Defence is more convincing than the points of Mr. Praljak, who is one part of the Defence?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, you have said the Defence. I meant the Prosecutor's side. What I meant to say was that of the two options that the president of the Court provided relating to the reports of Mr. Andric, this is what I want to say, and I apologise for my mistake.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just one last question and then Mr. Praljak will be able to proceed. When you have to do with a military offensive of the type you can see unfolding on the 9th of May, in such a setting, prior to the offensive, aren't there any orders being given, preparatory orders of logistics, material, various equipment, weaponry, health, doctors, orders that were to prepare for the attack, whether it was organised by the ABiH or the HVO? In 1993, so this is not back in the Middle Ages, that's only -- well, close to 14 years ago, back then, did you not have to prepare for an attack with orders, with preparatory orders, or was it done just casually, randomly. You were on the ground. You met with generals, with senior officers, with ministers. What was your feeling as to the factions and armies in presence? Were there professional armies that were able to prepare attacks according to the rules of warfare or were they doing just anything?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, obviously in 1993, both sides involved in the conflict had professionals with knowledge of the situation or with knowledge as to how to organise a military operation. UNPROFOR never received internal information as to what was being prepared, obviously not. We never had that information. Had we had that information, we would have passed it on to the appropriate authorities, to Kiseljak. I think that the management or direction of combat was not particularly good on either side, but the feeling, the general feeling in UNPROFOR was that the HVO side relied on its artillery to a large extent whereas the Armija had better infantry. Perhaps there was a lack of balance. In former -- in former combat against the Serbian army, this is what used to happen. Mostar is a different kettle of fish. Mostar is not an open battlefield. The artillery is not as useful and perhaps it was infantry that was needed most, but I am not familiar about the preparation for the attack. I do not know whether it was in fact an attack that took place simply because it was known that the generals in charge were not there, but General Pasalic in fact comes quickly in order to enter Mostar because he is in fact the one that brings together the 4th Corps of the Armija. And it is clear that the Armija did attack in the area of the Presidency, the president's building, and there was a large movement of troops and that UNPROFOR had to leave the area. All this is correct. All the information we had led us to believe that as professionals with more experience perhaps than the people there, led us to believe that the attack came from the HVO side, and this is why we wrote that. Otherwise we would have written something different.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Please proceed. THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: Sir, I'm interested in the following: Out of your people, who was in Mostar on the morning of the 9th of May? To cut this short we thought we concluded, we inferred, what have you not. In Mostar on the 9th of May who was where from SpaBat? Do you know or do you not know? Please don't look through these papers. Just tell me if you know or don't know?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DV [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the 9th of May in the morning, the unit stationed in Mostar left Mostar. This information I can give you. Also, I can give you that we got information from inside Mostar through some of the Spanish intelligence people who remained in Mostar, to protect soldiers, well, we have also elements that act isolated, and we receive information from these people.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] One moment. Please let me intervene because you said that already yesterday already and nobody picked that up or grasped the extent of what you were saying. You said that SpaBat left Mostar, but you also say on page 101 that there were elements that stayed. I was going to say were they spies for you who would give you information, or were they SpaBat members who had stayed inside Mostar under the guise of -- some guise, and who would inform you as the events were unfolding? Could you let us know how you had organised information to get to you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] On that day, or about that day, I have no details. However, elements of the reconnaissance patrols, command posts, specialised, with electronic means, could be in areas which were not controlled by any side but that could observe the situation. It's habitual practice in western armies, and of course we cannot discount the possibility that we had these. We cannot say whether we had more than two. I cannot say. THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: Please, could have, whatever. Really, we're speaking in the conditional now, what could have taken place. Electronic surveillance could have done this and that. Sir, this is a classical attack in the street, somebody either saw that or did not see that. If someone saw it, it could have happened only at a certain place at a certain time. Let us stick to logic. I am very well versed in Spanish literature. We can talk about Cervantes but this is not that. This is a military matter. Who concluded on the basis of what, on the basis of fact, that someone from the HVO started that attack in contravention of everything that I'm going to prove through the documents, but please look at your report on the 8th of May, number 36. On the 8th of May 1993, in the evening, we brought the British, French, and Spanish ambassadors to Mostar. Oh, yes, where Mate Boban was. They had a meeting with Mr. Stojic and Mr. Bozic. The meeting was held in the building of the Presidency of Herceg-Bosna. On the same day we secured an escort for Mr. Pasalic from Kiseljak to the eastern part of Mostar. So on the evening of the 8th of May, you sat in Mostar. You were there yourself, right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I was in Mostar.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: Yes. Now, an experienced soldier -- well first of all, if an offensive was being prepared for the 9th, why would they let you in on the 8th? Secondly, where is the army? The military is supposed to be there, preparations, mortars, rocket launchers, tanks. Aren't you a soldier? How can one get into Mostar near the actual front line that would later be attacked by the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and you don't see anything on the evening of the 8th? No one sees a thing? You talk quite peacefully with three ambassadors, everything is peaceful, calm, and the next morning, the HVO launches an attack, and you conclude that through electronic surveillance, how, who, where? Can you give me an answer to that? If not I would just like to deal with a few more documents and then we're going to move on to our next topic.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DV [Resumed]
utterances.text: The night of the 8th was a very surprising night for me because there were plenty of patrols and soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: Sir, please, tell me did you see any preparations on the evening of the 8th that were involved in an attack? Yes or no. Tell me that. Patrols were there for the ambassadors.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DV [Resumed]
utterances.text: My mission was to bring the APCs, take the ambassadors to the Presidency building and hand them over to Mate Boban. I waited two hours outside, and I had the opportunity of talking to some soldiers. I saw so military preparations or what I would consider military preparations. That is the answer. I saw no military preparation, correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you very much, sir. Please look at this document, we have 3D 01001. It says, "Around 1700 hours, an attack by the Bosnian army to get back to Hum was repelled." That's what is written here, do you know where Hum is? 3D 01001. You will see here even Babic got killed, and right under that, around 1700 hours, an attack -- an attempt of the BH army to climb the hill of Hum was repulsed. You have it on the screen, sir. If you wish you can have a look at the screen.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I have the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: Do you see that written there? Now that we are on the subject of Hum, you were still in Mostar at that time. Do you know about this major offensive of the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina on the 20th of September 1993, against West Mostar, inter alia against the hill of Hum, the 20th of September 1993? What do you know about that? If you don't know anything, then I'd like to move on.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sorry, I've misunderstood. You're talking about the 20th of September? You're talking about an attack against the hill on the 20th of September?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. There is a mistake here. The document is dated the 9th of May. It's a report which was drafted at 8.00 p.m. and this report explains that at 5.00 p.m. the HVO repelled an attack by the ABiH army which was trying to take control of the Hum hill. I think in military terms, this does mean the same thing. What do you have to say to this? Is it surprising? Is it normal? How do you react? How do you respond to this? I must say this is a bit of a quandary for me because we know that they were positioned on the hill of Hum, and if this attack took place, this attack must have been prepared beforehand. What do you have to say to this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, obviously, who controlled the Hum hill had a perfect vantage point over Mostar, so I could well understand that one side would have the control and others would try to storm or take over that control point. And we did have information whereby the attack against the Hum hill was taken place from Donja Mahala. I can confirm that this is true. THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Sir, now I wanted to ask you about a different date concerning an attack on Hum. I'm talking about the 20th of September 1993. Do you know about that attack of the BH army at Hum? Yes or no. Sir, you don't need to look at documents. Sir, please, just what you know. You were down there. Do you know, do you know that there was an attack launched by the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina on the 20th of September 1993 against Mostar, the hill of Hum, and so on? Do you know about that? Oh, all right. Let's skip that question. This is my last document, 3D 0 -- 3D 01000. That's the last one that has to do with this topic. 3D 01000.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DV [Resumed]
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: The 10th of May. Miljenko Lasic, because of a conflict between the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina and the HVO, he's asking for 82-millimetre mortars, 120-millimetre mortars and so on and so forth. And he's asking for that as urgently as possible. Can you see that document? Is this correct, what is stated here?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DV [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can see the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: 3D 01021, the last document. Miljenko Lasic --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DV [Resumed]
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: Is writing to the commander of UNPROFOR, Zagreb, the 10th of May 1993. Do you see the signature of Miljenko Lasic? And he says, "We are surprised by the totally unfounded assessment of UNPROFOR that allegedly HVO forces on the 9th of May 1993 started combat actions in Mostar and that in this way, they violated the three last agreements between Croat and Muslim commanders under the protection of the UN. We are surprised that Mr. Wahlgreen wasn't objectively informed about who actually did not respect the above-cited agreement and who, in fact, after numerous previous provocations, started combat actions precisely against the Tihomir Misic barracks located on the left bank of the Neretva River in which the BH army is already tidying up as an area where only Muslims will be living." He says that "The Republic of Croatia has nothing to do with it." And he also says, "It is true that the HVO units responded to combat action, of the BH army, with a single objective in mind, to defend the city and its population." Have you ever seen this document that was sent obviously through your UNPROFOR, Zagreb?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DV [Resumed]
utterances.text: From this document, our colonel head of operations had told us of it, but I don't think we ever actually saw the document itself. But I think we were aware that the document had been produced. I thought that it wasn't Lasic. I thought that it was Minister Stojic. That was what believed until now.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: Sir, do you know that on the 30th of June, the barracks of Tihomir Misic were attacked by the BH army inside and outside to cut things short, they took the barracks and they continued their combat operation a month later? Do you know about that? On the left bank of the Neretva near the railway station in the northern part of town? While we are waiting, could the usher please put this on -- oh, you know that, thank you.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. For us, for UNPROFOR, it was a known fact that the importance of the northern and southern barracks that enclosed the city were very important for both sides. I remember receiving information periodically concerning some.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: [No interpretation]? [Speakers overlapping] Time is running out.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a minute, Mr. Praljak. It is 4.00. We have to have a 40 [as interpreted] minute break now, and we shall resume at 20 minutes past 4.00 accused. THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation] Just have a look at these two photographs so that will be all right? Would that be possible?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In that case, all right, but very quickly, please. THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: Sir, please look at the photograph of this big building? Could it please be placed on the ELMO, the photograph of this building, oh just leave it, leave it on the ELMO. Sir, could you please put it where it was? Thank you, and I apologise to the interpreters. Is this the building where you went up when you were investigating the death of your officer?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DV [Resumed]
utterances.text: If my memory serves me correctly, it is this building, and can I have a pointer? And here, you can see the corner -- I think it's this corner, one moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: Mark that, please. Please mark that corner.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: The corner where you were.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DV [Resumed]
utterances.text: This photo doesn't actually help me very much because I saw it from the bridge, but I think that this is the building, and I think it was this part right here, you can see this top corner. This is where the house was where formerly we had the elevator.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: Please mark that. Please mark where that would be. Please put number 1 there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DV [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: Please, number 1, by that.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DV [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: So that is where you went up, and you saw something like an elevator and you found some casings; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DV [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no. There was no elevator. There was a hole at that point, and I think something would have been there beforehand. But yes we did find shells there.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: There could have been one, of course there wasn't a lift an elevator, but you were in that building in that place and you found a casing or casings; is that right? Would you place the date and your signature to the photograph? That's customary in this Court. Or rather your initials. You needn't write your name and surname. Your Honours would you explain to the witness what he should do?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please write in the initials DV, please, DV, and write today's date.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 2nd of October 2007.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Registrar, could we have an IC number, please?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours, the document shall be given Exhibit number IC 673. Thank you, Your Honour. THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: Now take a look at the second photograph. Can we see the entire photograph, please? Move it up a bit. Now, along this street, if you go down this street, by the cars, if you carry on further down to the left part of the photograph, would you get to Tito's bridge where there was an APC, a SpaBat APC, just draw in an arrow? You go down this street and you get to Tito's bridge; is that right? That's right, in that direction; is that correct? That Tito's bridge is to be found there? And if so, place an arrow, please.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DV [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: So following the direction of that arrow, you would find Tito's bridge; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DV [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: Witness, this photograph, well, along with the buildings, the buildings there today, nothing can be changed, but this photograph was taken from approximately the position or rather this photograph is more to the advantage in a way of the Prosecution, but my position is this: In no way, not then, not now, from that building, could you see the location at which your officer was located when he died. Is what I'm saying the truth or not? Is it a lie or is it the truth? And that's my last question before the break.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DV [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is incorrect. From the top of the building, there is another -- there is a different panorama, different visibility. I'm not saying that it's wrong. It's just that I filmed and photographed the panorama from the top of the building, and this was done at the time. It's not a recent piece of evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: But why haven't we got this panorama view, panoramic view?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The photograph was taken from the highest point, the one where you were standing. From there, one cannot see the bridge. That seems pretty obvious. What we see here, in the light of what we have here in front of us, we can't see the bridge on the photograph. So could one see the bridge from another vantage point in the building? Because you are saying that you could see the bridge from where you were standing.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The bridge exactly can be seen from what we call the left wing, which is the metallic bridge which goes into the Muslim part controlled by the Armija. That could be seen and the trees could be seen, yes. But this particular photo might be taken from the same building, but it has a completely different angle and it's not the same as what I saw. Both photos could be put side by side to compare the two. The Spanish Battalion, I know, has copies of the photos. I'm not sure about the video but the photos, yes. On top of that, the photos were sent to the national press and it was marked on the photo where the death occurred. But this photo, albeit taken in the same building, from the same building, it's neither the -- it shows neither the height that I remember or the position that I remember. I'm not saying that -- well, I'm just saying it doesn't actually show what I saw when I climbed the building.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We have to have a 20 minute break now. We shall resume at half past 4.00. Mr. Praljak, according to my calculation, there are 70 minutes left. How much time will you need after the break? THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation] Your Honour, as much as you give me. The question of the wounded, the injured, and perhaps the military situation which the gentleman is aware of.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We need to finish at 5 p.m. So please reflect on those questions which you wish to put to the witness and we should finish at 5.00 p.m. We shall now have a 20-minute break and resume at half past 4.00 sharp.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] First of all, I'd like to ask the Prosecution how much time they will need for their redirect.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: Your Honour, I don't think that I need it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Mr. Praljak, you still have 20 minutes. We will give Mrs. Alaburic five minutes for her additional questions and that will wrap it up. So you have 20 minutes left. THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. That's going to be sufficient for my purposes. I hope that we will see the photograph that the Spaniards took and that the Prosecution will make it available to us. Could we mark this one the same way we marked the previous one, with initials and a date?

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: Would you mark it, please, Witness? Could you please initial this photograph and your secret initials, that is, and then could we have the date, today's date?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DV [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Could we have an IC number for this photograph, registrar, please?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] Your Honour, the document shall be given Exhibit number IC 674. Thank you, Your Honour. THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: Witness, would you look at your diary, P02108, now, please, and we'll go through some things and look at the 27th of August 1993, that entry?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DV [Resumed]
utterances.text: 27th of August, yes, I have it.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: Look at the end of the page in Croatian, the departure of five children plus four relatives from the Muslim part of Mostar in order to go to Split by helicopter, plane from Split, Zagreb, Mec. Now, that evacuation was can carried out?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It was conducted.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, do you remember the evacuations that went from East Mostar, UNPROFOR transport to Medjugorje, a helicopter to Split and then further on to Turkey by plane? Do you remember those evacuations? Just to go through them quickly now.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DV [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were many evacuations during my time in the task force, I don't know which ones you're referring to, but I remember the process of evacuations, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: They are the ones that went to Turkey. We have the documents from earlier on but now take a look at your diary, and the entry of the 1st of September 1993 when the evacuation was agreed upon to Mostar and Nova Bila. Do you remember that, that the agreement reached was about parallel evacuations? Or simultaneous evacuations from Nova Bila, that is Croats there and Mostar and the other wounded?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DV [Resumed]
utterances.text: I recall the problems that we had in getting people out of the hospital in Mostar, yes, and Nova Bila.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: Now, look at that same document, the entry for the 3rd of September 1993. This is what it says, or what you say here. That the HVO completed its evacuation to Split, two helicopters, and then you say that the evacuation from Mostar by helicopter to Zenica was not carried out because of the bad weather conditions. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. If that's in my personal diary? What I have on the 3rd of September is that the agree [as interpreted] was concluded and then there was -- there was the Nova Bila evacuation and the one from Mostar was abandoned because of bad weather, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: Very well. Now take a look at the 6th of September. This is what you say. 31 wounded persons were transported, that's the first evacuation, to Zenica. Then on the 7th of September, the evacuation of 3 children and their mothers from Jablanica. On the 8th of September, the evacuation of 38 wounded persons by helicopter from East Mostar. Then the 10th of September, it says -- no, the 8th, there was a medicines transport to both parts of Mostar, and the main UNHCR office to East Mostar, then we come to the 11th of September entry, 34 wounded persons from the Muslim part were evacuated from Medjugorje to Zenica by helicopter together with five wounded prisoners who were in the HVO hospital at Bijeli Brijeg. And then that same date, and then we have the 12th of September, the evacuation of 38 persons, wounded Muslims from the Muslim hospital in Mostar, taken to Medjugorje, transported by helicopter to Zenica. Is all that correct? Everything it says there, is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DV [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is correct, and it reflects the summaries.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, may we have on e-court P04857, please? P04857 is the document number. It is a report dated the 7th of September 1993, signed by Dr. Ivo Sandrk. It will appear on e-court. And while we are waiting for the document to come up on our screens, I'd like to ask you the following: Sir, did you ever, were you ever prevented by the HVO from carrying out any person from East Mostar or Jablanica, mother, a child, a woman, the wounded, anybody? Were there any obstacles to pulling those people out, for your mission to take place, the transport of wounded persons to Medjugorje, were there any attempts to prevent that or make it impossible in any way, any obstacles at all?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely not. I remember the positive attitude that I met with in order to carry out the evacuations. I was grateful for it at the time and I'm grateful now.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness. Now take a look at the next document, if -- P04857, if we have it up on our screens. Anyway, it's a long document, I won't be able to look at all of it but with Dr. Sandrk according to what we have in our records, you talked to Dr. Sandrk. Did you negotiate with him and Thornberry and the other people at these meeting held on the 1st of September 1993 and the 2nd, 3rd of September, the 4th, 5th, et cetera, did you attend those meetings? You confirm this earlier on but once again we have it here.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes. I believe that I recalled that Dr. Bagaric was in charge of the hospital, and so I think the medical part of the HVO, I can't remember in detail, but I had many meetings in the hospital. And I remember that everything was carried out quite frankly under good conditions.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: It says here on the 4th of September, well, the second page in the Croatian text of this document, that Dr. Mira Camidzic, a lady doctor was seriously wounded and transferred to the HVO hospital and from thence to Split. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DV [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, this particular fact, no, I don't but remember from Mostar to Split it was quite an easy transfer. It was quite easy to make that transfer.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: Yes, of course. Now look at the next sentence, Sandrk says, "I'm going to Mostar in order to be present when the MOS wounded were loaded up. There was an MOS attack on the town controlled by the HVO." On that occasion, 18 civilians were wounded, of which five children. There were five fatalities, two children amongst them. And among the wounded civilians, eight were Muslims, eight persons were Muslims. It is quite clear that the attack had, as its aim, to depict MOS to the public in that way and that the evacuation could not have been carried out for security reasons. On that same day, two helicopters evacuated 29 seriously wounded HVO members to Split and some ten children from Nova Bila. Do you remember that mortar attack?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I remember -- and I think it wasn't the only attack. I remember, yes, that there was a problem on several occasions, security problems.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: This document, among other things, says that the Muslim side kept changing its negotiating team, that Dr. Milavic did not appear and so on and so forth. Did you ever notice at those meetings that the HVO were in a moment -- that it wasn't ready to do everything in its power so that the wounded citizens or injured citizens should be pulled out and taken to Zenica or Mec, the American hospital in Zagreb or to Croatian hospitals? You answered this earlier on, but did you ever notice that there was not the readiness on the part of the HVO to do anything like that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DV [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Absolutely not. I found that they were fully available, and I always came across people with the appropriate authority to solve the problems, the concrete problems, that we encountered at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: Thank you. I have one more document now. At the beginning, you said that you weren't sure what I was doing in July, August, and September over there. Do you know which position I had in the HVO in July, August, and September? What was my post, function?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DV [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't say that I didn't know what you were doing in July, August, and September. I said I didn't know where you were on the 11th of May. That's what I was asked. Later with the information we received through the local press, we inferred what your rank was and that you were in charge of military coordination of activities. As for your exact post, I wasn't familiar with that. But I remember that I have the videos and you met with other generals, with General Petkovic, but I didn't know your official title.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: Now, sir, tell me this: Since, as you say, you had your -- well, let's call them spies or people who provided you with information, since you had a battalion with a lot of officers, how come you didn't know that I was the commander of the Croatian Defence Council? Isn't that a little strange, that an organisation like your own, with so many information sources about what was going on in Mostar, whereas in the space of three and a half months, you weren't able to obtain information about what I was? And I was the commander of the Main Staff of the Croatian Defence Council, the HVO. That's what I'm telling you. How is that possible? That's my first question. Can you explain to the Court how that is possible?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DV [Resumed]
utterances.text: I reiterate that we didn't have a copy of your official title. We knew that you had an important post and that you could deal with problems that came up, for example, evacuations, et cetera, but we didn't know what your exact title was, your exact post.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: And tell me this, please: Which press, local press, existed at the time in the area? Give me the name of any paper that you could have read at the time.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Just a correction. I didn't read the papers. It was my interpreters who read the local press. It was the interpreters who read the local press, whatever local press that was available that they could get their hands on. And at that time there was no internet there at that time, so we didn't have that access to information, I'm not sure, but I remember that we bought three or four publications.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: Now, sir, you say that you received information from your interpreters. Now, to learn about what the Main Staff commander did and his existence, you learnt about that through interpreters and some local press, which, actually, did not exist there. Is that right? Is it right that the information -- that information about my function and position --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Could you enlighten the Chamber as to the relevance of these questions? I do not quite see where in the indictment they find any root, nor do I find them very pertinent as far as the credibility of the witness is concerned. THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation] Your Honour, they are linked to the credibility of information. The information coming in from the battalion, which numbers almost 2.000 people, which is a professional army within NATO, and they say that information about the main operative part of the army, the head of it, that he learnt that from interpreters reading the -- reading the local press.
